Senses.PreferredTarget: a mud ox bellowing at the moon
AlternateTargets: mud ox bellows at the moon

ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: A mud ox bellowing at the moon gives voice and upward address to an earthen animal that cannot move or cry. Chan masters pair it with a wooden horse neighing in the wind, use it in questions about Chan and the Way, and place it in verses where ordinary causal expectations are suspended.
EvidenceBody: Yinyuan Longqi pairs “the mud ox bellows at the moon” with “the wooden horse neighs in the wind.”
Meixi Du’s interlocutor asks whether the mud ox and wooden horse constitute the Way; Meixi answers with the paired sand-and-water saying.
Gaofeng Yuanmiao’s verse makes the mud ox face the wind and bellow at the moon while warning against a mistaken fixed measure.
Yuancheng’s hall address brings a one-legged mud ox bellowing at the moon beside a three-headed wooden horse.
Yichu Yuan says the mud ox opens the gold-lock barrier while the wooden horse breaks the silver mountain iron wall.

Senses.Note: Fifty-two exact hits occur in thirty-seven frozen works. Five witnesses preserve fixed pair, public question, capping verse, one-legged variant, and barrier predicate.
